beats.headline: Why does your batch job crash at 20 million rows?
beats.subline: Loading everything into memory is a rookie mistake. Here is how to process massive datasets safely.
beats.narration: If you load 20 million rows into a list, you will trigger an OutOfMemoryError instantly. Spring Batch solves this with chunk-oriented processing, streaming your data in small, manageable bites.

beats.title: Naive Loop vs. Chunked Pipeline
beats.narration: The naive loop pulls everything into RAM and holds a database lock for hours. The chunk approach processes items in small batches, committing to the database incrementally.

beats.title: The Chunk Cycle
beats.subtitle: Read, Process, Write, Commit
beats.narration: The reader pulls one item, the processor transforms it, and the writer buffers them until the chunk size is hit. Only then does the transaction commit, ensuring data consistency.

beats.title: Writing Chunks in Spring Batch 5

steps.explanation: Spring Batch 5 uses the Chunk container instead of a simple List.
Access the buffered items to perform your bulk database operations.

beats.narration: In Spring Batch 5, the writer receives a Chunk container. This is your signal to perform bulk operations, keeping database round-trips to a minimum.

beats.title: Part 1 Locked In
takeaways: Never load full datasets into memory
Chunk size is a memory/throughput trade-off
Use Chunk<T> for Spring Batch 5 writers

beats.headline: What happens when one bad row kills your job?
beats.subline: Don't let a single malformed record roll back hours of work. Use declarative skip policies.
beats.narration: One malformed row can crash a 10-hour job. You need a strategy to isolate the failure, log it, and keep the rest of the pipeline moving.

beats.title: Configuring Fault Tolerance

steps.explanation: Use for transient errors like network blips or deadlocks.
Use for data validation errors that will never succeed.

beats.narration: Retry is for transient infrastructure issues. Skip is for data errors. By setting a skip limit, you prevent a bad data explosion while still allowing the job to finish.

beats.title: The Scanning Mode Mechanism
beats.subtitle: How Spring Batch isolates failures
beats.narration: When a chunk fails, Spring Batch rolls back and enters scanning mode. It re-processes items individually, committing valid ones and isolating the poisoned record for your listener.

beats.title: Dead-Letter Strategy
beats.caption: Always log skipped items to a table!
beats.narration: Never skip silently. Use a SkipListener with REQUIRES_NEW propagation to save the bad record to a dead-letter table. This ensures you can audit failures after the job finishes.

beats.title: Part 2 Locked In
takeaways: Retry for infrastructure, Skip for data
Always use a SkipListener for auditing

beats.headline: Does your job know where it left off?
beats.subline: Spring Batch tracks every execution in the database. Here is how to resume after a crash.
beats.narration: If your server crashes at 2:00 AM, you don't want to restart from zero. Spring Batch uses the JobRepository to track state, allowing you to pick up exactly where you left off.

beats.title: Metadata Persistence
beats.subtitle: The JobRepository schema
beats.narration: The JobInstance defines the logical run. Each attempt is a JobExecution. The ExecutionContext stores the commit count, so the reader knows exactly which record to fetch next.

beats.title: The Paging Trap

steps.explanation: Use a monotonic ID range to avoid skipping rows during status updates.

beats.narration: Be careful with status flags. If you update rows to 'PROCESSED' while reading, your offset shifts and you will skip data. Always use a stable keyset range for paging.

beats.title: Resuming a Job
beats.caption: Metadata enables automatic resume
beats.narration: Just relaunch the job with the same parameters. Spring Batch detects the failed execution, loads the context, and resumes from the last committed chunk automatically.

beats.title: Part 3 Locked In
takeaways: Relaunching with same params enables resume

beats.headline: One thread isn't enough?
beats.subline: Partitioning splits your workload into parallel slices. Here is how to scale across CPU cores.
beats.narration: When one thread hits a performance wall, don't just optimize. Partition the workload. Split your data into logical slices and process them in parallel.

beats.title: Partitioning Strategy
beats.subtitle: Manager vs Worker steps
beats.narration: The manager step calculates ID ranges. Each worker gets its own context and reader, running in parallel. If one worker fails, only that partition needs a restart.

beats.title: StepScope Reader

steps.explanation: Creates a new reader instance for every partition.
Injects the partition-specific minId into the query.

beats.narration: Use @StepScope to create a unique reader for every worker. The SpEL expression pulls the range bounds directly from the partition's execution context.

beats.title: Scaling Checklist
beats.caption: Align your resources!

lines.text: # 3. Ensure DB indexes on sort keys

beats.narration: Scaling is a balancing act. Match your grid size to the thread pool, increase your database connection pool, and ensure your sort keys are indexed, or your workers will just stall.

beats.title: Chapter Complete
takeaways: Align thread pools with database connections
